Simulation study: do the weights recover known effects?

Source: vignettes/articles/simulations.Rmd
simulations.Rmd

The new weights in ipw recover known causal effects when their model is correct, and the naive or misspecified alternatives are clearly biased. This article shows that with a simulation study in the spirit of the simulated example in the JSS paper (van der Wal & Geskus 2011): each scenario generates data in which the true marginal causal effect is known, estimates it, and repeats this many times.

How the results were produced. The study is in dev/simulation-study.R in the repository; the code below shows the essential lines of each scenario. It takes several minutes, so this page shows saved results rather than running it. To reproduce them, run Rscript dev/simulation-study.R in the package folder (seed 20261101), or start the simulations workflow from the GitHub Actions tab. Scenarios 1 to 4 use 500 replications, 5 and 6 use 250, and 7 uses 100 with 200 bootstrap samples each.

Reading the tables. Bias is the mean estimate minus the truth; empirical SD is the spread of the estimates over replications; RMSE combines both. A good method has bias close to 0 and a small RMSE.

1. ATE, ATT and overlap weights, and ipwprob()

The effect of a binary exposure varies with the confounder l, so the three estimands differ. Their true values, computed from 2 million simulated people, are ATE = 1, ATT = 1.276 and ATO = 0.861. Each weighting scheme is compared with its own target; ipwprob() is given the true propensity scores.

d <- data.frame(l = rnorm(1000))
d$a <- rbinom(1000, 1, plogis(0.5 + 0.8 * d$l))
d$y <- d$a * (1 + d$l) + d$l + rnorm(1000)
w.att <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                  denominator = ~ l, data = d, estimand = "ATT")$ipw.weights
coef(lm(y ~ a, data = d, weights = w.att))["a"]
Method Truth Mean estimate Bias Empirical SD RMSE Replications
unweighted (target ATE) 1.000 1.989 0.989 0.114 0.995 500
ATE weights 1.000 1.002 0.002 0.089 0.089 500
ATT weights (target ATT) 1.276 1.275 -0.001 0.107 0.107 500
ATO weights (target ATO) 0.861 0.864 0.002 0.082 0.082 500
ipwprob, true probabilities (ATE) 1.000 1.006 0.007 0.144 0.144 500

All weighted estimates are unbiased for their own estimand; the unweighted difference is nearly twice the ATE.

2. Count exposure: Poisson or negative binomial

The exposure is an overdispersed count (negative binomial, variance larger than the mean); each extra unit raises the outcome by 0.5.

d <- data.frame(l = rnorm(1000))
d$v <- rnbinom(1000, size = 2, mu = exp(0.5 + 0.4 * d$l))
d$y <- 0.5 * d$v + d$l + rnorm(1000)
w.nb <- ipwpoint(exposure = v, family = "negbin", numerator = ~ 1,
                 denominator = ~ l, data = d)$ipw.weights
Method Truth Mean estimate Bias Empirical SD RMSE Replications
unweighted 0.5 0.671 0.171 0.022 0.172 500
poisson weights (misspecified) 0.5 0.329 -0.171 0.078 0.188 500
negbin weights (correct) 0.5 0.507 0.007 0.038 0.039 500

The negative binomial weights are unbiased. The Poisson model ignores the overdispersion, and its weights over-correct: the bias is as large as that of the unweighted analysis, in the other direction.

3. Skewed continuous exposure: gaussian, gamma or log-normal

The dose is log-normal given l; one unit of dose raises the outcome by 1.

d <- data.frame(l = rnorm(2000))
d$dose <- exp(0.5 + 0.5 * d$l + rnorm(2000, 0, 0.6))
d$y <- d$dose + 2 * d$l + rnorm(2000)
w.ln <- ipwpoint(exposure = dose, family = "lognormal", numerator = ~ 1,
                 denominator = ~ l, data = d)$ipw.weights
Method Truth Mean estimate Bias Empirical SD RMSE Replications
unweighted 1 1.534 0.534 0.042 0.536 500
gaussian weights (misspecified) 1 1.130 0.130 0.085 0.156 491
gamma weights (misspecified) 1 0.983 -0.017 0.165 0.166 500
lognormal weights (correct) 1 1.061 0.061 0.087 0.106 500
lognormal weights, truncated 1% 1 1.179 0.179 0.036 0.183 500

The log-normal weights remove most of the confounding, with a small remaining bias (0.06) that is typical of weights for continuous exposures: the density ratio has a heavy tail. The gaussian model is clearly biased, and in 9 of 500 replications gave infinite weights, which ipwpoint() refuses. The gamma model happens to have little bias here but twice the spread. Truncation at the 1st and 99th percentiles reduces the spread a lot but adds bias: the usual trade-off.

4. Curved propensity: smooth terms with mgcv

The probability of exposure depends on l through a sine curve; the true effect is 2.

d <- data.frame(l = runif(2000, -2, 2))
d$a <- rbinom(2000, 1, plogis(2 * sin(1.5 * d$l)))
d$y <- 2 * d$a + 3 * sin(1.5 * d$l) + rnorm(2000)
w.gam <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                  numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ s(l), data = d)$ipw.weights
Method Truth Mean estimate Bias Empirical SD RMSE Replications
unweighted 2 4.547 2.547 0.093 2.548 500
linear logistic weights (misspecified) 2 2.659 0.659 0.086 0.665 500
s(l) weights 2 2.070 0.070 0.064 0.095 500

A straight-line logistic model leaves about a quarter of the confounding bias in place; s(l) lets mgcv estimate the curve and removes almost all of it.

5. Time-varying ordinal dose, type = "all"

A dose level (0, 1, 2) is chosen at each of 4 visits from a proportional-odds model given the confounder L and the previous dose. L is affected by the previous dose and by an unmeasured U, which also affects the outcome. The outcome rises by 1 per unit of cumulative dose. This is the situation in the JSS paper where ordinary adjustment fails: L is both a confounder and affected by earlier treatment.

for (t in 1:4) {
  l <- U + 0.4 * prev + rnorm(n, 0, 0.5)
  dose <- findInterval(0.8 * l + 0.6 * prev + rlogis(n), c(0, 1.5))   # 0, 1, 2
  prev <- dose
}
y <- 1 * cumulative.dose + 2 * U + rnorm(n)

w <- ipwtm(exposure = dose, family = "ordinal", link = "logit",
           numerator = ~ dose.lag, denominator = ~ dose.lag + l,
           id = id, timevar = time, type = "all", data = long)
# weight at the last visit, then lm(y ~ cumulative.dose, weights = ...)
Method Truth Mean estimate Bias Empirical SD RMSE Replications
unweighted 1 1.492 0.492 0.035 0.493 250
regression adjustment for L 1 0.855 -0.145 0.028 0.147 250
ordinal weights (correct) 1 1.027 0.027 0.110 0.113 250
multinomial weights 1 1.010 0.010 0.116 0.117 250

The unweighted analysis is confounded, and adjusting for L at every visit is biased in the other direction, because it blocks part of the effect and opens a path through U. Both ordinal weights (the correct model) and multinomial weights recover the effect.

6. Recurrent exposure events, family = "survival", type = "all"

Exposure events (for example new prescriptions) happen repeatedly with a known proportional hazard: baseline 2 per unit time, log hazard ratio 0.5 for a fixed covariate x and -1 for a time-varying covariate xt. Because the true hazard is known, the true weights are known too, so the check is on the Cox coefficients and on how close the estimated weights are to the true ones. In 6a all people share a grid of 10 intervals (as in haartdat); in 6b the events happen in continuous time, xt changes at different times for each person, and each event ends an interval (start-stop data cut at events, as in Graffeo et al. 2018).

w <- ipwtm(exposure = expo, family = "survival", denominator = ~ x + xt,
           id = id, tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime, type = "all", data = d)
coef(w$den.mod)
median(abs(log(w$ipw.weights / true.weights)))
Method Truth Mean estimate Bias Empirical SD RMSE Replications
Cox coefficient of x 0.5 0.499 -0.001 0.084 0.083 250
Cox coefficient of xt -1.0 -0.983 0.017 0.099 0.100 250
median |log(estimated / true weight)| 0.0 0.069 0.069 0.020 0.072 250
Cox coefficient of x 0.5 0.500 0.000 0.091 0.091 250
Cox coefficient of xt -1.0 -0.996 0.004 0.093 0.093 250
median |log(estimated / true weight)| 0.0 0.091 0.091 0.024 0.094 250

The Cox coefficients are unbiased in both designs, and the estimated weights are typically within 7 to 9% of the true weights, which is the estimation noise of the baseline hazard.

7. Standard errors: ipwboot() versus robust standard errors

The marginal structural model for a binary exposure (true effect 10, n = 500) is fitted with stabilized weights; 95% confidence intervals come from ipwboot() (200 bootstrap samples, re-estimating the weights) or from robust standard errors (survey::svyglm). In 7a, exposure probabilities are mostly between 0.1 and 0.9 (good overlap); 7b is the simulated example of the JSS paper, where the logit of the propensity has a standard deviation of 5, so many people are almost certain to be exposed or unexposed.

msm.effect <- function(dd) {
  w <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit", numerator = ~ 1,
                denominator = ~ l, data = dd)$ipw.weights
  coef(lm(y ~ a, data = dd, weights = w))["a"]
}
ipwboot(d, msm.effect, R = 200)
Scenario Method Mean estimate Mean SE Empirical SD Coverage of 95% CI Replications
7a. good overlap ipwboot, percentile CI 10.054 0.492 0.457 0.95 100
7a. good overlap robust SE (svyglm), Wald CI 10.054 0.539 0.457 0.95 100
7b. JSS example (poor overlap) ipwboot, percentile CI 11.323 1.072 1.632 0.50 100
7b. JSS example (poor overlap) robust SE (svyglm), Wald CI 11.323 1.060 1.632 0.53 100

With good overlap, both intervals reach their nominal 95% coverage; the robust standard error is about 18% larger than the true spread of the estimates and the bootstrap about 8%, in line with Austin (2016). In the JSS example, the estimate itself is biased at this sample size (11.3 instead of 10) and both standard errors are far too small, so coverage is only about 50%. Near-violations of positivity, not the choice of standard error, are the problem there: check the weights (summary(), ipwplot()) and consider overlap weights or truncation.

References

  • Austin PC (2016). Variance estimation when using inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) with survival analysis. Statistics in Medicine 35, 5642-5655.
  • Graffeo N, Latouche A, Geskus RB, Chevret S (2018). Modeling time-varying exposure using inverse probability of treatment weights. Biometrical Journal 60, 323-332.
  • Li F, Morgan KL, Zaslavsky AM (2018). Balancing covariates via propensity score weighting. Journal of the American Statistical Association 113, 390-400.
  • van der Wal WM, Geskus RB (2011). ipw: An R package for inverse probability weighting. Journal of Statistical Software 43(13), 1-23.
